name: Kong Empire
summary: A Muslim Dyula trading state in today’s northern Ivory Coast, linking gold and kola from the forest with the Niger trade; destroyed by Samori Touré in 1897.

location.value: A pre-colonial state centred on north-eastern Ivory Coast, also covering parts of Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana.

terrain.value: Open savanna with scattered trees and rivers.

climate.value: Tropical, with a rainy season and a long dry season with dusty harmattan winds.

resources.value: Kola nuts from the forest to the south, gold, cotton and dye for cloth, and farmland.

disasters.value: Droughts and the famines that followed them.

population.value: Kong town had perhaps 15,000 people in the 1800s, according to the French explorer Binger.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Dyula (Mande) merchants settled in trading towns across the region.

economicBase.value: Kong became a centre of trade in gold and kola nuts; the page does not name cloth or slaves as trade goods.

tradeRoutes.value: Linked the forest kola and gold areas in the south with the Niger bend markets (Djenné and Timbuktu) in the north.

wealth.value: Rich Muslim merchant families controlled trade and lent money.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A largely decentralised commercial empire, the Wattara (Ouattara) empire, that became a constellation of mostly separate fiefdoms each ruled by a Watara clan member, with local government under military commanders called kuntigi.

keyRulers.value: Seku Watara, a Dyula who had studied the Qur’an, founded the dynasty in 1710 by deposing Lasiri Gbambele; his brother Famagan and Famagan’s son Kere-Mori secured the Mouhoun bend, and Famagan’s campaign of November 1739 took Sofara and besieged Ségou.

succession.value: Within branches of the Wattara family, which often divided territory.

institutions.value: The Wattara warrior rulers, Muslim scholar families and merchant households.

stability.value: Central control was weak; the northern branch became a separate kingdom.

eliteConflict.value: Rival branches of the Wattara family.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and infantry, with muskets bought through trade.

majorWars.value: Samori destroyed the city on either 23 May 1897 or 18 May 1898; the infobox gives only 1898.

territoryChange.value: Expanded north towards Bobo-Dioulasso and east towards Gyaaman in the 1700s.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of Asante and Gyaaman in the trade of the south; later threatened by Samori and the French.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Very open to traders and Muslim scholars from across West Africa.

communicationTransport.value: Donkey and porter caravans along savanna trade routes.

religion.value: A key commercial centre and centre of Islamic studies; Dyula merchants were largely Muslim, the Senufo and Tyefo mainly animist, and Islam did not shape how the ruling aristocracy ran the state.

languageWriting.value: Dyula (Jula), a Mande trade language; Arabic for religion and letters.

artsArchitecture.value: Mud-brick mosques in the Sudano-Sahelian style, such as the great mosque of Kong.

socialStructure.value: Wattara warriors, Muslim merchants and scholars, Senufo and other farmers, artisans and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Dyula Muslim merchant identity alongside loyalty to the Wattara.

dailyLife.value: Families farmed millet and yams in villages; towns lived from trade, weaving and markets.

neighbours.value: Asante, Gyaaman, Gonja, the Mossi kingdoms and Senufo peoples.

ideasReligions.value: A centre of Islamic learning, with Quranic schools run by scholar families.

colonisation.value: Binger signed a treaty with Kong (1889); after Samori’s attack the area became part of French Ivory Coast (1898).

riseSignals.value: Founded in 1710 by Seku Watara (also written Sekou); capital Kong.

peakPeriod.value: The 1700s, when Kong controlled the trade routes and Wattara rule reached Bobo-Dioulasso.

outcome.value: Samori Touré attacked and destroyed Kong in 1897 or 1898 (the article gives both dates); the French then took control of the area.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
